prompt: A photo site serves the same images to users on every continent, and users far from the US data center wait seconds for images to load.
tells: far from the US data center
why: Identical static files and distant users: serve them from CDN edges close to each user.
trap: A server-side cache still sits in one region. The problem is distance, not computation.

prompt: A course platform streams pre-recorded videos, and bandwidth costs from the origin servers are exploding.
why: A CDN serves the bytes from its edges, so most traffic never reaches the origin.
trap: A queue moves work around. It doesn't serve video bytes.

prompt: A news site's article pages are identical for every reader, and a breaking story sends traffic up 100× overnight.
why: Cache whole pages at the edge so the origin barely notices the spike.
trap: Rate limiting would turn readers away during your biggest moment.

prompt: Your web app's JavaScript and CSS bundles are fingerprinted per release and never change between deploys, but first loads are slow abroad.
why: Immutable files and users far away: serve them from a CDN with long cache headers.
trap: A fingerprinted file never changes, so the edge can cache it for good.

prompt: A game studio releases a 60 GB patch that millions of players download in the first hour.
tells: millions of players download in the first hour
why: Huge identical files spread across many edge locations so no single server takes the load.
trap: Rate limiting would just make players wait. A CDN adds capacity.

prompt: Your marketing site is hit by a traffic flood from many IP addresses, and you want the origin to stay up without changing app code.
tells: traffic flood from many IP addresses
why: A CDN's edge network absorbs the flood (and can filter it) before it reaches your origin.
trap: Rate limiting inside your app still means every request reaches your servers, and it needs code changes.

prompt: A maps feature serves pre-rendered tiles, and the same tiles for popular cities are requested by everyone.
why: Identical, pre-built files: a textbook CDN case.
trap: An in-app cache avoids rebuilding the tiles, but every request still travels to your servers.

prompt: A podcast host serves MP3 files that never change after publishing, and listeners worldwide complain about buffering.
why: Static audio files and a global audience: serve them from the edge.
trap: Read replicas move database queries closer to users, not files.

prompt: A static marketing site gets visitors from every continent and must load fast everywhere.
why: Static files served from edge locations near each visitor.
trap: An in-memory cache next to your origin is still one ocean away from most users.

prompt: A game studio will release a 2 GB trailer at a set time and expects millions of downloads in the first hour, worldwide.
tells: millions of downloads in the first hour
why: Identical bytes to millions of people at once: let edge servers absorb the bandwidth.
trap: Object storage holds the file, but serving millions of downloads from one region is the bottleneck.

prompt: A shop's product images are the same for every visitor and make up 80% of its bandwidth bill.
why: Offload identical static bytes to the edge; origin bandwidth drops sharply.
trap: Moving images to object storage changes where they live, not how far they travel.
